summary: Lunar Light Clock shows when the Sun and the Earth are visible from three candidate landing sites near the Moon's south pole (Shackleton rim, Nobile rim, Malapert summit). It combines the NASA LRO LOLA 20 m elevation model with JPL Horizons positions of the Sun and Earth, ray-marches a 360 degree terrain horizon at each site, and tells a mission planner, hour by hour, whether a lander has power and a direct radio link to Earth. A browser viewer (no install) lets you slide through dates, click any point to score it, compare sites and see what changes if the landing slips. Every number is checked against NASA's published LOLA visibility maps, over a full 18.6-year cycle (2026-2044) and with a Monte Carlo test of DEM error, so planners know how far to trust it.
details:
What it does: Near the Moon's south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a few metres of terrain decide whether a lander has power, and Earth is often below the horizon too, so a direct radio link is not guaranteed. On the Shackleton rim the Sun stays below the horizon for up to 147 hours in a row in 2027. Lunar Light Clock answers, per site and per hour: is the Sun up, is Earth up, and for how long are both missing.

How it works: our Python pipeline reads the NASA LRO LOLA LDEM_85S_20M_FLOAT south polar DEM, takes a 64 km window around each site resampled to 40 m, and ray-marches a 360 degree horizon (rays up to 30 km, 2 m observer, sphere curvature). Hourly Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation come from JPL Horizons. A body is visible when its elevation is above the terrain horizon at its azimuth. A static three.js viewer shows the 3D terrain, horizon, Sun and Earth tracks, a date slider, a Navigator (click any point, get its Sun and Earth score, choose 0/2/5 m observer height, export CSV), a landing-window planner with a "what if it slips" view, an Earthset countdown and Sun-elevation sonification.

Results (2027): Shackleton rim Sun 86.0%, longest darkness 147 h, Earth 45.9%; Nobile rim Sun 88.0%, 151 h, Earth 59.1%; Malapert summit Sun 64.6%, 341 h, Earth 79.5%. The trade-off is clear: Malapert keeps Earth in view, Shackleton and Nobile keep the Sun.

Validation: we compared our values with the NASA/LOLA-team AVGVISIB_85S_060M_201608 average visibility maps (Sun: -0.8, +5.1, +7.9 points; Earth: -7.8, -0.6, -5.0 points). An independent horizon code agrees within 0.09-0.12 degrees on average. A multi-year run over 2026-2044 (a full 18.6-year cycle) moves Sun fractions by 2.9-3.1 points and Earth by 4.9-9.6 points. A Monte Carlo test of DEM vertical error moves Sun fractions by 0.3-1.6 points. Observer height is the biggest factor. Limits: terrain beyond 30 km is ignored, so Sun fractions are upper bounds; read results as about plus or minus 10 points. Full numbers: docs/validation.md in the repository.

Benefits and impact: mission planners, students and the public can compare candidate sites in seconds, in a browser, with honest error bars, instead of working through complex GIS tools. Tools: Python (numpy, astropy, astroquery, matplotlib), JavaScript and three.js, GitHub Pages. 18 automated tests pass.

Presentation PDF (7 pages): https://github.com/RizgarOzan/albedo-spaceapps/blob/build/docs/pdf/Albedo_LunarLightClock.pdf
